directAnswer: St. Cornelius was the twenty-first bishop of Rome, elected in March 251 after the Church had gone more than a year without a bishop during the Decian persecution. His pontificate was defined by the controversy over readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution, in which he upheld reconciliation after penance against the rigorist Novatian. Exiled by Emperor Gallus, he died at Centumcellae in 253 and is honored as a martyr.

paras: After Pope Fabian was martyred in January 250, the persecution of Decius made it impossible for the Roman Church to choose a successor, and the presbyters governed collectively for over a year. When the pressure eased, Cornelius was elected in March 251. St. Cyprian of Carthage later wrote that he had risen through all the ranks of the clergy and had not sought the office, but accepted it under pressure.

His election was immediately challenged. Novatian, a gifted Roman presbyter and theologian who had written an important treatise on the Trinity, had himself consecrated as a rival bishop and is counted among the antipopes.

sections.h2: The Lapsed and the Schism of Novatian
paras: The central issue was how to treat the lapsed, Christians who had offered sacrifice or bought certificates to escape punishment under Decius. Novatian held that the Church could not grant them reconciliation; only God could forgive them. Cornelius, in agreement with Cyprian and most bishops, held that they could be received back after suitable penance.

Cornelius convened a synod in Rome of about sixty bishops, which condemned Novatian and his followers and confirmed the policy of readmitting the repentant. Synods in Africa and elsewhere took the same line. Novatian’s community nonetheless survived as a separate church for several centuries.

Cyprian at first hesitated to recognize Cornelius until he was sure of the facts, then became his firm supporter. Their surviving correspondence is one of the richest sources for the Church of the mid-third century and for relations between Rome and Carthage.

sections.h2: A Snapshot of the Roman Church
paras: In a letter to Bishop Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, Cornelius describes the clergy of Rome to show how absurd it was for Novatian to claim the office. He lists forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers, and says the Church supported more than fifteen hundred widows and people in distress.
These figures make the letter one of the most valuable records of how a major Christian community was organized before Constantine, and they suggest a Roman Church numbering many thousands.

In 252, under Emperor Trebonianus Gallus, persecution resumed and Cornelius was banished to Centumcellae, the port now called Civitavecchia. Cyprian wrote to congratulate him on his steadfast confession. Cornelius died there in June 253, and the Church regards his death from the hardships of exile as martyrdom.

His body was later brought to Rome and buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, in a separate crypt where his tomb bears a Latin inscription naming him a martyr. He is named in the Roman Canon, and his feast is kept on September 16 together with St. Cyprian.

keyFacts: Twenty-first bishop of Rome, March 6, 251, to June 253
Upheld reconciliation of the lapsed after penance against Novatian
Roman synod of about sixty bishops condemned Novatian
His letter to Fabius of Antioch records the size of the Roman clergy
Died in exile at Centumcellae (Civitavecchia); buried in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus
Named in the Roman Canon; feast day September 16 with St. Cyprian

faqs.question: What was the Novatian schism?
faqs.answer: Novatian, a Roman presbyter, opposed Pope Cornelius’s policy of readmitting Christians who had lapsed during persecution, insisting the Church had no power to reconcile them. He was consecrated as a rival bishop and condemned by a Roman synod, but his rigorist church survived for centuries.

faqs.question: Why are St. Cornelius and St. Cyprian celebrated together?
faqs.answer: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, supported Cornelius against Novatian, and they corresponded closely. Both died for the faith within a few years of each other, and the Church honors them together on September 16.

faqs.question: Was Pope Cornelius killed for his faith?
faqs.answer: He was not executed. He was exiled to Centumcellae under Emperor Gallus and died there in 253, and the Church honors his death in exile as martyrdom.
